title: Virtual Memory, Paging and Cache Locality
oneLiner: Latency numbers every engineer should know, why iterating a 2-D array row by row beats column by column, and how a virtual address becomes a physical one.
keyTakeaway: Memory moves between RAM and the CPU caches in 64-byte cache lines, so touching neighbouring addresses is nearly free and jumping around is expensive: an L1 hit costs about 1 ns and a trip to RAM about 100 ns. Programs see virtual addresses, which the CPU translates page by page (usually 4 KB) through the page table, cached in the TLB. A page that is not in RAM causes a page fault, and the OS has to step in.
explanation:
Computer Architecture (in Computer Fundamentals) introduced the hierarchy: registers, caches, RAM and storage, each level bigger, cheaper and slower than the one above. This lesson is about what that means for the code you write. A modern core can execute several instructions per nanosecond, but a read that misses every cache waits about 100 ns for RAM. Without caches, the CPU would spend almost all its time waiting.

Caches never fetch a single byte. They fetch a whole cache line, 64 bytes on x86 and most ARM chips, the 16 ints around the one you asked for. Programs that use nearby data soon after (spatial locality) or reuse the same data soon (temporal locality) get most of their reads from cache. A C# int[,] stores its rows one after another (row-major order), so looping over rows on the outside and columns on the inside walks memory sequentially and uses all 16 ints of every line. Swap the loops and each access jumps a whole row ahead, landing on a different line every time; once the matrix is larger than the cache, almost every access misses. Same algorithm, same Big O (the growth-rate measure covered in Data Structures & Algorithms), often 5 to 10 times slower. This is also why arrays usually beat linked lists in practice, even when both are O(n): list nodes are scattered across the heap, so every step can be a miss.

Multithreading has its own cache trap, false sharing. Caches keep cores consistent at cache-line granularity, so two threads that each update their own counter, if the counters happen to share one 64-byte line, still force that line to bounce between cores on every write. The fix is to pad or space the counters into separate lines, or give each thread a local counter and combine at the end.

Virtual memory gives every process the illusion of its own large, private address space. The address your program uses is virtual; the CPU's memory management unit (MMU) splits it into a page number and an offset within the page (4 KB pages means the low 12 bits are the offset), looks the page number up in the process's page table to find the physical frame (the page-sized slot of real RAM that holds it), and keeps recent translations in the TLB (translation lookaside buffer) so most lookups are free. Two processes can use the same virtual address and reach different physical memory, which is how the OS isolates them, and why a process switch costs more than a thread switch: the TLB's translations belong to the old process.

If the page table says a page is not in RAM, the CPU raises a page fault and the OS takes over. A minor fault just needs a frame assigned (the first touch of freshly allocated memory, or a page already cached by the OS). A major fault has to read the page from disk, thousands of times slower than RAM; a machine that is constantly doing this is thrashing. An address that is not mapped at all is an access violation (a segmentation fault on Linux) and the process is killed.
